abstract: Background: Personalized targeting of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) based on functional connectivity (FC) to the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) is promising for depression treatment, but direct evidence that precisely engaging an individually defined FC target produces specific downstream modulation is lacking. Objective: To test whether stimulating individually defined cortical targets with strong negative or positive FC to sgACC/ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) produces target- and network-specific downstream BOLD effects compared to nearby control targets. Methods: Twenty healthy participants underwent concurrent TMS-fMRI. For each participant, we identified a dorsolateral PFC target with strong negative FC and a dorsomedial PFC target with strong positive FC to sgACC/vmPFC as well as control targets with weaker sgACC/vmPFC-FC strength, but matched peripheral co-stimulation experience. Coil positions and orientations were optimized using electric field simulations. Single TMS pulses were applied during concurrent fMRI, and BOLD responses were compared between conditions. Results: Stimulation of negative FC targets produced significantly stronger negative BOLD modulation in sgACC/vmPFC and dorsomedial PFC compared to control targets. Positive FC targets showed no significant differences from controls. The spatial pattern of negative FC target-related BOLD effects significantly resembled a previously described convergent depression circuit, while positive FC targets produced an anticorrelated pattern. Conclusions: Personalized precision TMS targeting produces target- and network-specific downstream effects, supporting the mechanistic premise of FC-guided TMS.
